content: BET theory is a fundamental principle used to describe the physical adsorption of gas molecules onto a solid surface. This theory was first introduced in 1938 by Stephen Brunauer, Paul Hugh Emmett, and Edward Teller, whose initials form the acronym BET. The theory extends the Langmuir adsorption model, which is limited to monolayer adsorption, to account for multilayer adsorption. The key assumptions of BET theory are as follows: (a) gas molecules can adsorb onto a solid surface in an infinite number of layers; (b) there are no interactions between molecules in different adsorption layers; and (c) the Langmuir adsorption model can be applied to each individual layer. The BET equation, which describes this adsorption process, is expressed as follows: ( v_m ) is the quantity of gas required to form a monolayer on the surface. ( c ) is the BET constant, which is related to the heat of adsorption and is defined as: [ c = expleft(frac{E_1 E_L}{RT}right) ] Here, ( E_1 ) is the heat of adsorption for the first layer, ( E_L ) is the heat of adsorption for subsequent layers (equal to the heat of liquefaction), ( R ) is the gas constant, and ( T ) is the temperature. The BET equation is an adsorption isotherm, and experimental data can be plotted as a straight line by graphing ( frac{1}{v} ) on the y-axis and ( phi = frac{P}{P_0} ) on the x-axis. This graph is known as a BET plot.05 and 0.35. From the slope (( A )) and y-intercept (( I )) of the BET plot, the monolayer adsorbed gas quantity (( v_m )) and the BET constant (( c )) can be calculated using the following relationships: ( v_m = frac{1}{A + I} ) ( c = 1 + frac{A}{I} ) The BET method is extensively used in surface science to calculate the surface area of solids by measuring the physical adsorption of gas molecules. The total surface area (( S_{total} )) and specific surface area (( S )) of a material can be determined using the following equations: ( S_{total} = v_m cdot N cdot s ) ( S = frac{S_{total}}{m} ) Here, ( N ) is Avogadro's number, ( s ) is the adsorption cross-sectional area of a single gas molecule, and ( m ) is the mass of the sample. By measuring the amount of water vapor adsorbed at various levels of relative humidity, a BET plot can be generated. From the slope (( A )) and y-intercept (( I )) of the plot, the monolayer adsorbed gas quantity (( v_m )) and the BET constant (( c )) can be calculated. For example, in the case of cement paste hardened in water at 97°C, the slope is ( A = 24.20 ) and the y-intercept is ( I = 0.33 ). Using these values, the specific BET surface area (( S_{BET} )) can be calculated. Assuming that one water molecule covers an area of ( s = 0.114 , text{nm}^2 ), the specific surface area of the hardened cement paste is found to be ( S_{BET} = 156 , text{m}^2/text{g} ). This indicates that the internal surface area of the cement paste is 156 square meters per gram of material. Application to Activated Carbon Activated carbon, a material known for its strong adsorption properties, typically exhibits a high surface area. For instance, experimental data for nitrogen adsorption at liquid nitrogen temperature reveal that activated carbon has an adsorption cross-sectional area (( s )) of ( 0.16 , text{nm}^2 ) and a surface area of approximately ( 3000 , text{m}^2/text{g} ). In the field of solid catalysis, the surface area of catalysts is a critical factor influencing catalytic activity. Porous inorganic materials, such as mesoporous silica and layered clay minerals, often exhibit high surface areas in the range of several hundred ( text{m}^2/text{g} ) when calculated using the BET method. This highlights their potential for use as efficient catalytic materials.
